Hydrogen Bonding: Look for H Bonded to F, N or O

Learning Objective: Recognize the X–H bonds that allow hydrogen bonding in the examples.

X–H···Y

Find the bond to H

HF · F–H

NH₃ · N–H

H₂O · O–H

  • Look for H directly bonded to F, N or O. In X–H···Y, X is the atom directly bonded to H.
  • HF has F–H, NH₃ has N–H, and H₂O has O–H. Each can form hydrogen bonds with neighboring molecules of the same substance.
  • The dotted line shows H interacting with a nearby F, N or O that has an available lone pair.
Topic T9.8 · Local Slide 3

Water Forms a Hydrogen-Bond Network

Learning Objective: Identify the solid O–H bonds and dotted attractions in a group of water molecules.

Hydrogen bonds link neighboring water molecules

  • Follow a gold dotted line. It starts at H on one water molecule and points to O on the next.
  • Many such attractions link water molecules in liquid water. The links continually change as the molecules move.
  • Heating to boiling lets water molecules separate from the network. The solid O–H bonds stay intact.
Topic T9.8 · Local Slide 4

Dipole–Dipole Attraction Between Polar Molecules

Learning Objective: Use overall molecular polarity to identify dipole–dipole attraction.

Two HCl molecules

Quick contrast · CO₂

The linear shape cancels the bond dipoles. CO₂ has no permanent molecular dipole.

  • HCl has a permanent molecular dipole. Cl carries δ⁻ and H carries δ⁺.
  • A favorable orientation brings opposite partial charges closer. This is dipole–dipole attraction.
  • Use the polarity of the whole molecule. A polar bond alone cannot establish a permanent molecular dipole.
  • London dispersion also acts between polar molecules. The next slide shows how it arises.
Topic T9.8 · Local Slide 5

London Dispersion Starts With a Fluctuation

Learning Objective: Explain how temporary dipoles attract neighboring particles.

A temporary imbalance

  • Electrons fluctuate in an atom or molecule. For a moment, one side can have more electron density.
  • The temporary dipole shifts electron density in a neighboring particle. Opposite partial charges face each other.
  • London dispersion acts between all atoms and molecules, including polar molecules.
  • Polarizability measures how easily an electron cloud distorts. More polarizable clouds generally give stronger dispersion. Shape affects how closely surfaces can approach.
